topics.title: Dancing Girl Controversy
bullets: A controversy has erupted over the NCERT’s decision to modify the image of the Harappan “Dancing Girl” in its Class 9 Arts Education textbook, sparking a debate on historical accuracy versus contemporary sensibilities.
The modified image showcased the bronze figurine with its torso covered, giving the impression that she was clothed, which led to a massive backlash from historians and educationists.

Following widespread criticism and a report by The Indian Express, the NCERT reversed its decision and restored the original image in the digital and upcoming print editions of the textbook. Background –
Also known as the Indus Valley Civilization, it was one of the world’s earliest urban cultures, flourishing around 2600-1900 BCE in the northwestern regions of South Asia.
It was a highly advanced society with planned cities, sophisticated drainage systems, standardized weights and measures, and extensive trade networks.
The civilization left behind a rich material culture, including sculptures, seals, pottery, and jewellery, but its script remains undeciphered, leaving many aspects of its culture a mystery.
Mohenjo-daro, located in present-day Sindh, Pakistan, was one of the largest settlements of the Indus Valley Civilization, known for its advanced urban planning and architecture.
The site was discovered in 1922 by archaeologist Rakhaldas Banerjee, and subsequent excavations revealed a wealth of artifacts that reshaped our understanding of ancient Indian history.
Among its most famous discoveries is the small bronze statuette known as the “Dancing Girl”.
The Dancing Girl was discovered in 1926 inside a small house at the Harappan site of Mohenjo-daro by British archaeologist Ernest Mackay.
The figurine is a 10.8 cm (or 10.5 cm) high bronze statuette of a woman, with her head tilted backwards and her knees slightly bent.
This diminutive statue, now housed in Delhi’s National Museum, has elicited countless interpretations since its discovery.

The Dancing Girl was made using the lost-wax casting technique, a sophisticated metallurgical process that involves creating a wax model, covering it with a mold, and then pouring molten metal into the cavity left after the wax is melted out.
This technique, which is still used in many parts of India today, demonstrates the advanced metallurgical skills of the Harappan people nearly 4,500 years ago.
The meticulous craftsmanship of the Dancing Girl suggests that it was not created for utilitarian purposes but as a symbol of cultural or artistic significance.
The name “Dancing Girl” was given by John Marshall, the Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India during the 1926 excavation.
Marshall named her so because he thought she had the “air of a semi-impudent ‘nautch girl’, beating time to the music with her feet”.
The label, rooted in colonial perceptions, has stuck, even though her posture doesn’t explicitly indicate dancing.
She has a completely bare torso except for a necklace and numerous bangles, 24-25 bangles on her left arm and four on her right.
The asymmetrical decoration of more bangles on the left arm than the right has led to speculation that the right arm may have been kept free for labour or even war.
Her hair is tied in a bun, and her posture captures the human body in motion, reflecting great artistic value.
The figure’s akimbo posture (hands on hips) with her right arm resting on her hip and left arm on her thigh is a key characteristic.
The same akimbo posture has been found on at least two potsherds from the Harappan site of Bhirrana in Rajasthan, suggesting it held a precise cultural value.
The Dancing Girl is often described as having a confident and poised expression.
In the absence of textual records, the figurine’s exact meaning and purpose remain speculative.
The lack of a deciphered Indus script means that we can only guess at the cultural and religious significance of such artifacts.
This ambiguity has led to a wide range of interpretations, from ritualistic to secular, each offering a different lens through which to view the figurine.
Some scholars have tried to view the figurine through a lens of ritualistic importance, drawing linkages with the idea of the mother goddess.
This interpretation suggests that the figurine may have been a symbol of fertility or a deity worshipped in the Harappan religion.
However, this view is not universally accepted, as there is no definitive evidence linking the figurine to any specific religious tradition.
More recently, there was an attempt to establish a connection between the Hindu goddess Parvati and the bronze figurine.
This interpretation draws on the idea that where there is Shiva (manifested in the “Proto-Shiva” seal), there should be Shakti (Parvati).
Some scholars have even claimed that the Harappan civilization worshipped Shiva, using the Dancing Girl as evidence of a proto- Parvati figure.

Another historical interpretation pertains to whether the figurine represented a warrior as the left arm’s fist isn’t fully closed— rather, there is an empty socket as if she is holding something (like a spear).
The figurine’s nudity has been a point of contention, with some viewing it as a natural representation of the human form in ancient art.
She has been described by archaeologist Mortimer Wheeler as his favourite statuette. Recent News –
The controversy erupted when the newly introduced Class 9 Arts textbook, Madhurima, featured an altered depiction of the Dancing Girl.
In the published image, the figurine’s torso was shaded over from the shoulders down, obscuring anatomical details and giving the impression that she was clothed.
The image was altered using shading, effectively “covering up” the bare torso of the ancient bronze sculpture.
Unlike the Class 9 version, the Dancing Girl image in the NCERT’s Class 6 Social Science textbook appeared in a form closer to the original bronze sculpture.
This inconsistency raised questions about why the image was retouched for the older students (Class 9) but not for the younger ones (Class 6).
The modified image was used in the opening chapter, “History of Arts”, of the new Arts Education textbook.
Historians and educationists accused the NCERT of disfiguring the iconic artefact and altering history.
Michel Danino, head of NCERT's Class 6 Social Science textbook committee, was told the Dancing Girl figurine was "not age- appropriate" for students.
He stated that the modification “misrepresents the original artefact”, comparing it to the Church’s addition of a fig leaf to Michelangelo’s statue of David.
The review of earlier editions by The Indian Express found that the “Dancing Girl” has appeared in NCERT textbooks for at least 25 years, including during the NDA government.
In all those years, the figurine’s torso had never been censored in any way.
This long history of uncensored use made the 2026 modification particularly significant and controversial. NCERT –
The National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) is an autonomous organisation set up in 1961 by the Government of India.
It assists and advises the Central and State Governments on policies and programmes for the qualitative improvement of school education.
NCERT is the country's apex advisory body on school education, shaping curricula, publishing textbooks, training teachers, and driving educational research.
One of its major functions is to prepare and publish textbooks as per the syllabus based on the recommendations of the National Curriculum Framework (NCF).
NCERT was formed through the merger of seven institutions after independence, including the Central Institute of Education (1947).
In 2026, the Ministry of Education declared NCERT a 'Deemed to be University’. This grants NCERT academic autonomy to design and run its own UG, PG, research, and doctoral programmes.

topics.title: e-OCI Card
bullets: On 30 June 2026, the Government of India launched the Electronic Overseas Citizen of India (e-OCI) card, a digital version of the OCI card introduced in August 2005.

The e-OCI platform allows eligible overseas Indians to complete the entire OCI application process online, from filling out the form and uploading documents to downloading the e-OCI card once approved.
The new system will benefit over 50 lakh OCI cardholders worldwide and streamline the application process for millions of overseas Indians. Background –
The Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card was introduced in August 2005 as a long-term visa and residency status for people of Indian origin living abroad.
It provides several benefits, including multiple-entry, multi- purpose, lifelong visa for visiting India and exemption from registration with the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO).
However, OCI cardholders are not Indian citizens and do not have voting rights, the right to hold constitutional office, or the right to purchase agricultural land.
An OCI card can be applied for by any foreign national who was a citizen of India on or after 26 January 1950, or belonged to a territory that became part of India after 15 August 1947.
It is also available to children, grandchildren, and great- grandchildren of such individuals.
Spouses of Indian citizens or OCI cardholders are also eligible, subject to certain conditions.

Benefits of the OCI Card – ➢Lifelong, multiple-entry visa for visiting India. ➢Exemption from registration with the FRRO for any length of stay in India. ➢Parity with Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) in economic, financial, and educational fields (except in matters relating to the acquisition of agricultural/plantation properties). ➢OCI cardholders can also open bank accounts, buy property (except agricultural land), and work in India (except in government jobs).
Before 2015, India had two separate categories: OCI Card and Person of Indian Origin (PIO) Card.
In January 2015, the Government of India merged the PIO card with the OCI card to simplify the system for overseas Indians.
Existing PIO cardholders were encouraged to convert their cards to OCI cards, and new applications were only accepted for OCI cards.
Before the e-OCI system, OCI applications required extensive paper documentation, physical submission at VFS Global Centres, and long processing times.
Applicants had to visit VFS Global centres in person for biometric submission, document verification, and to collect the physical OCI card.
This process was time-consuming, expensive, and inconvenient for overseas Indians, especially those living in countries without easy access to VFS centres.
The new e-OCI system is designed to simplify and streamline online processing, reduce paperwork and costs, and improve data management.
It integrates well with digital immigration systems for real-time checks at airports, ensuring better identity verification and reducing the chance of fraud.
The transition to e-OCI is part of India's broader "Digital India" initiative, aimed at making government services more accessible and efficient. Citizenship (Amendment) Rules, 2026 –
On 30 April 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) notified the Citizenship (Amendment) Rules, 2026, updating the Citizenship Rules, 2009.
Under these rules, OCI applications must now be filed online. This change was a precursor to the full e-OCI system.
The amendments came into force immediately upon publication in the official gazette on 30 April 2026.
The Citizenship Rules, 2009 were framed under Section 18 of the Citizenship Act, 1955, which empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act.
The rules provide the procedural framework for acquisition, determination, and renunciation of citizenship, as well as the registration of Overseas Citizens of India (OCI).
The 2026 amendments represent the most comprehensive restructuring of these procedures since the rules were first notified.
The Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) scheme was introduced in 2005 through an amendment to the Citizenship Act, 1955.
It allows registration of Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs) as OCI cardholders if they were citizens of India on or after 26 January 1950, or were eligible to become citizens on that date.

However, individuals who are or have been citizens of Pakistan or Bangladesh, or whose parents, grandparents, or great-grandparents held citizenship of these countries, are not eligible under the scheme.
A major policy clarification added in Rule 3 states that a minor child cannot, at any time, hold the passport of any other country while also holding an Indian passport.
The words "at any time" have been added afresh to the provision, reinforcing that dual passport holding by minors is strictly prohibited.
Applicants are required to formally acknowledge this condition, and a corresponding declaration has been added to the related form.
For a minor child born outside India, the applicant must submit a declaration that the child does not hold a passport of any other country.
If the child is already holding a foreign passport, they cannot simultaneously hold an Indian passport.
The applicant must also submit the birth certificate of the child issued in the country of birth, together with the declaration.

Under clause (da) of Section 7D of the Citizenship Act, 1955, OCI registration shall be liable for cancellation when a person has been sentenced to imprisonment for two years or more or has been charge-sheeted for an offence punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more.
The MHA had issued a notification on 11 August 2025 clarifying these cancellation grounds.
The revised Rule 35 now empowers the Centre to treat an e-OCI registration as cancelled by direction, even without physical card surrender.
The amended rules introduce a new provision in Schedule 1C of the 2009 rules requiring applicants to declare and surrender passports issued by Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Bangladesh.
This requirement applies to citizenship applicants from these countries seeking Indian citizenship.
The amendment aims to streamline documentation and strengthen procedural compliance for applicants from these nations.
The amended Rule 42 restructures the appellate process for citizenship matters.
Citizenship applicants aggrieved by an order may now approach an authority one rank higher than the original deciding authority.
This ensures a fair and transparent mechanism for challenging adverse decisions.
A new Rule 42A separately provides for the review of orders under the newly inserted Section 15A of the Citizenship Act.
For OCI-related grievances, the Central Government will designate the revision authority
The new rules have also simplified forms and procedures for citizenship applications. Recent News –

On 30 June 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs launched the Electronic Overseas Citizen of India (e-OCI) card, marking a significant achievement in harnessing technology to improve governance and public service delivery.
The e-OCI is a new digital version of the OCI card that allows applicants to complete the entire application process online.
Applicants can now fill out their application, upload documents, and download the e-OCI card once it is approved.
Under the new Citizenship rules, eligible foreign nationals are no longer required to be resident in India for six months before submitting an OCI application.
They can submit the application soon after arrival in India if they have a valid long-term visa.
OCI cardholders who obtain a new passport must update their passport details on the OCI portal within three months of issuance.
OCI status does not confer Indian citizenship.
OCI cardholders cannot vote, cannot hold public office, and cannot apply for an Indian passport.
They are not eligible for constitutional posts (President, Vice- President, Judge of SC/HC).
The application fee for OCI registration is US $275.
PIO cardholders converting to OCI are charged a reduced fee of US $25.
The e-OCI card was launched alongside the FCRA 2.0 Portal by Union Home Minister Amit Shah.
The e-OCI card is not a physical card but a digitally authenticated document that can be downloaded and printed by the applicant.
It contains a QR code and other security features to ensure authenticity and prevent forgery.
The e-OCI system will benefit more than 50 lakh OCI cardholders worldwide.
Fully online application process – no need to visit a VFS (Visa Facilitation Services) Global Centre except for specific document verification.
Real-time tracking – applicants receive an acknowledgement number and can track their application status online.
Reduced processing time – the digital system is expected to significantly reduce the time taken to process OCI applications.
Under the new e-OCI system, OCI booklet holders will no longer be required to obtain a new OCI booklet upon issuance of a new passport after attaining the age of 20.
Previously, re-issuance was required up to age 20 and again after 50 years.
Applicants need to fill out Form XXVIII, providing personal information such as name, date of birth, and contact details. Official portal: OCIservices.gov.in.

Eligibility Criteria – ➢Former Indian citizens who renounced Indian citizenship. ➢Persons of Indian origin (PIOs) whose parents, grandparents, or great-grandparents were citizens of India. ➢Spouses of Indian citizens or OCI cardholders. ➢Minor children of eligible OCI applicants. Passage: In 2026, an NCERT textbook sparked controversy after references to the famous Dancing Girl bronze figurine of the Harappan Civilization were revised in a manner that generated academic and political debate. Historians, archaeologists, and educators expressed differing views regarding the interpretation of archaeological evidence and the presentation of ancient Indian history in school textbooks. The Dancing Girl, discovered at Mohenjo-daro in present-day Pakistan, is one of the most iconic artefacts of the Indus Valley Civilization. Cast using the lost- wax technique, the bronze sculpture reflects the advanced metallurgical skills and artistic achievements of the Harappan people. The controversy also revived wider discussions regarding urban planning, trade, script, craftsmanship, and the decline of the Harappan Civilization. Source: Indian Express The famous Dancing Girl bronze figurine was discovered at: A. Harappa B. Dholavira C. Mohenjo-daro D. Lothal
